# Week 7, Day 2.1 - Prerequisites check

**Almost no new TypeScript today** - Day 2 is about how APIs work, not about the language.

| In play | Taught in |
|---|---|
| Objects, nested objects | [week3/day1_1](/learn/w3/d1/p1) |
| `JSON.parse`, and `any` | [week5/day5_1](/learn/w5/d5/p1) |
| Template literals | [week6/day3_1](/learn/w6/d3/p1) |
| `enum` | [day1_2](/learn/w7/d1/p2) |

One shape is worth five minutes, because every API answer arrives in it.

## JSON is key/value, and it nests

| Rule | Example |
|---|---|
| Keys are always quoted strings | `"title": "Git Pocket Guide"` |
| Strings quoted, numbers not | `"pages": 234` |
| `[...]` is a list | `"books": [ ... ]` |
| A value can be another object | `"data": { "id": 2 }` |

The nesting is what trips people up: to reach a child you must name every parent.

// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Skipping a level is the most common error

`parsedBody.title` is `undefined`, because `title` is a child of an item of `books`. And the
error message you eventually get blames the wrong line.

Read that message carefully: it complains about reading `title` **of undefined**, so the thing
that was missing is `data` - the dot *before* the one named in the error.

Remember that inversion. It is the single most common way to waste ten minutes on an API test:
the error names the property you asked for, never the one that was absent.

# Week 7, Day 2.2 - What an API is

Six weeks of this course drove a browser. Today the browser goes away and you talk to the server
directly - which is faster, earlier, and how most testing work is actually heading.

> **Mode: mixed.** Explore cells use `fetch`; one cell writes and runs a real spec.

## The testing pyramid, and why anyone cares

| Level | What it checks | Cost of a bug found here |
|---|---|---|
| Unit | one function's logic | lowest |
| **Integration / API** | modules talking to each other | low |
| System / UI | the whole thing through a browser | high |
| Acceptance / UAT | a human agrees it is right | highest |

The pyramid says: many tests at the bottom, few at the top. Most teams do the opposite - and then
find bugs at the UI level, where fixing one means re-coding, re-testing and re-regressing.

The trend the session quotes: **~30% of coverage through the UI, ~70% through the API.**

## Why API tests are worth more per test

| | UI test | API test |
|---|---|---|
| Needs a browser | yes | **no** |
| Typical duration | ~30 s | ~3 s |
| Breaks when a button moves | yes | no |
| Can run before the UI exists | no | **yes** |
| Language of the app matters | no | no |

**Roughly 10x faster.** 2000 tests at 30 s is over 16 hours; at 3 s it is under two.

## What API tests cannot do

Worth being honest about, because "100% API" is a bad goal:

| Not testable through an API | Why |
|---|---|
| Colours, layout, spelling on screen | there is no screen |
| A confirm dialog - "Are you sure?" | that is browser chrome |
| The browser Back button | there is no browser |
| Visual regression | see [week4/day5_2](/learn/w4/d5/p2) |
| That a real person can complete the journey | the whole point of UI tests |

## Request and response - the whole model

Two things travel. That is it.

| Direction | Carries |
|---|---|
| **Request** | a verb, a URL, optional headers, optional body |
| **Response** | a status code, and usually a body |

And any URL splits into three parts:

```
https://demoqa.com/BookStore/v1/Books
-----   ----------  ------------------
protocol   host          endpoint
```

The endpoint is also called a **microservice** - one service among many at that host.

## CRUD is four verbs

Every application does four things to data. HTTP has a verb for each.

| Do | Verb | Body? |
|---|---|---|
| Create | `POST` | **yes** |
| Read | `GET` | no |
| Update | `PUT` (whole) / `PATCH` (part) | **yes** |
| Delete | `DELETE` | usually no |

`GET` and `DELETE` carrying no body is the detail that catches people out - see
[day4_2](/learn/w7/d4/p2), Step 6.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Status codes come in four families

Remember the **family**, not the number. The first digit is the part that is reliable.

| Family | Means | Whose problem |
|---|---|---|
| **2xx** | it worked | nobody's |
| **3xx** | it moved - look at `Location` | nobody's |
| **4xx** | your request was wrong | **yours** |
| **5xx** | the server broke | **theirs** |

Two results from that run deserve your attention.

**Step 3 - the session predicts 404 and the API answers 400.** Both are 4xx. The exact number is
the developer's choice; the family is the contract. Never assert a code you have not seen.

**Step 6 - a 200 that means failure.** Sending a wrong password to `GenerateToken` returns:

```json
{ "token": null, "expires": null, "status": "Failed", "result": "User authorization failed." }
```

Status `200`. Verified live.

## So: always two verifications

| Check | Answers |
|---|---|
| The status code | did the server accept the request? |
| The body | did it do the right thing? |

A test that checks only the status passes on Step 6's response. That is the rule this whole
lesson exists to install.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Asserting only the status code | Step 6 passes your test while the login failed |
| Assuming 404 for "not found" | this API says 400; assert what you probed |
| Following redirects and never noticing | use `maxRedirects: 0` to see the 3xx |
| Sending a body with `GET` | ignored at best, rejected at worst |
| Treating 5xx as your bug | it is a bug report, not a test fix |

# Week 7, Day 2.3 - Reading the documentation

Nobody hands you a list of endpoints. You get a docs page, and how quickly you can read it decides
how quickly you can test.

## Swagger / OpenAPI

Most APIs publish an interactive page - request shape, response shape, and a **Try it out**
button that fires a real call from the browser.

| Live example | Style |
|---|---|
| [demoqa.com/swagger](https://demoqa.com/swagger/) | Swagger UI - the API this week uses |
| [api.spreecommerce.org](https://api.spreecommerce.org/) | a large, very polished reference |
| [restful-booker apidoc](https://restful-booker.herokuapp.com/apidoc/index.html) | the API week8 uses |

Both of the first two are live right now; open one alongside this lesson.

## What to extract, in order

For any endpoint, six questions. Answer them before writing a line of code.

| # | Question | Where it usually is |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which verb? | the coloured badge |
| 2 | What URL, and what goes in it? | the path, with `{id}` placeholders |
| 3 | Does it need auth? | a padlock, or a `token` parameter |
| 4 | What must the body contain? | "Request body", with required fields marked |
| 5 | What comes back on success? | the 2xx example response |
| 6 | What comes back on failure? | the 4xx examples - **usually the thinnest section** |

Question 6 is where docs are weakest, which is why you probe.

## The docs are a claim, not a fact

Read, then verify. This is the habit that separates an API tester from someone typing out
examples.

Three calls, three behaviours, and only the first is prominent in the documentation:

| Call | Status | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| a known ISBN | 200 | as documented |
| an unknown ISBN | **400** + a message code | **not** the 404 most people would guess |
| no ISBN parameter at all | **500**, and an HTML error page | **a bug in the API** |

That third row is worth reporting. A missing required parameter is a *client* mistake, so the
honest answer is a 4xx; a 500 means the server fell over trying to read something that was not
there. And the body is HTML, not JSON - so a test that called `.json()` on it would fail with a
parse error and blame itself.

This is what "read the docs, then probe" buys you: two of those three behaviours are not written
down anywhere.

// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Authentication versus authorization

Two words people use interchangeably. APIs do not.

| | Authentication | Authorization |
|---|---|---|
| Question | who are you? | are you allowed? |
| Typical proof | username + password | a **token** |
| How often | once, to get a token | on every single request |
| This API | `POST /Account/v1/GenerateToken` | `Authorization: Bearer <token>` |

A token is like an OTP: short-lived proof it is you, handed over instead of your password.

## Monolith or microservices

The architecture behind the endpoint, and the reason "endpoint" and "microservice" get used
interchangeably.

| | Monolithic | Microservices |
|---|---|---|
| Shape | one deployable application | many small services |
| Deploying a change | often the whole thing goes down | one service restarts |
| Failure | everything stops | one feature stops |
| Attack surface | small | **larger - every service is a door** |
| Testing consequence | few, broad endpoints | many narrow ones, and the gaps between them |

The session's analogy earns its keep in one line: a corner shop closes entirely to refit; a mall
closes one unit. That is why your bank can say "transfers unavailable 1-2am" while the rest of
the site works.

For a tester the practical upshot is the last row: **the interesting bugs move to the seams
between services**, which is exactly where API tests live.

## Where the data comes from

| Layer | Holds |
|---|---|
| Presentation | the UI |
| **Business / API** | the rules, and the routes between the other two |
| Data | the database |

Static pages come from an app server, rows from a database server, and large media often from a
separate host entirely - which is why one page can be fast and slow at the same time.

# Week 7, Day 2.4 - Practice

problems.statement:
**Collect one of each family**
Find a real request that returns a 2xx, a 3xx, a 4xx and a 5xx. Print status and URL for each.

**Right when:** four different families, and for the 3xx you can also print the `Location`
header.

**Break the URL three ways**
Take `https://demoqa.com/BookStore/v1/Books` and break it: wrong host, wrong path, wrong query
parameter name.

**Right when:** you can say which failed at the network level and which returned an HTTP error -
and why those are different problems.

**Find another 200-that-means-failure**
Hunt for a second endpoint that returns a success status with a failure body.

> Hint: authentication endpoints are the usual offenders.

**Right when:** you can show the status and the body side by side.

**Read the docs, then check them**
Pick any endpoint from `demoqa.com/swagger/` that this week has not used. Answer the six
questions from [day2_3](/learn/w7/d2/p3), then call it.

**Right when:** you have all six answers and can name one thing the docs did not tell you.

**Watch a redirect happen**
Request `https://the-internet.herokuapp.com/redirect` twice - once following redirects, once with
`redirect: "manual"`.

**Right when:** you get two different statuses and can explain which one a test should assert on.

**Time it**
Time an API call to `/BookStore/v1/Books`. Then time a Playwright UI test from any earlier week.

**Right when:** you have two numbers and a ratio - and can say whether the session's "10x" holds
up for you.

**Token expiry**
Generate a token, then use it. Now find out how long it stays valid.

> Hint: the response has an `expires` field. Read it rather than waiting.

**Right when:** you can state the lifetime and say what a suite should do about it.

**Draw your own line**
For an application you know, list five things you would test through the API and three you would
insist on testing through the UI.

**Right when:** each of the three has a reason from [day2_2](/learn/w7/d2/p2)'s "cannot do" table.
